text: In the last lesson you met random variables and expected value. Now we meet the small family of distributions that show up again and again whenever you count things: orders returned, tickets received, visitors who convert. A distribution is just a rule that says how likely each possible outcome is — for a discrete variable, that rule is a probability mass function, listing a probability for every whole-number outcome.

A Bernoulli variable has two outcomes, 1 for success and 0 for failure, with success probability p — one customer either returns an order or doesn't. Its mean is p and its variance is p times 1 minus p. With p equals 0.3, scipy's bernoulli gives a mean of 0.3 and variance of 0.21.

Repeat a Bernoulli trial n times and count the successes — that's binomial. Suppose 10 orders ship today, each with a 30 percent chance of being returned. pmf of 3 gives the chance of exactly 3 returns, about 26.68 percent. cdf of 3 gives the chance of 3 or fewer, about 65 percent. sf of 4, the survival function, gives the chance of more than 4 — about 15 percent for 5 or more returns.

The binomial assumes trials are independent and p stays the same every time. If returns cluster — one bad batch ruins several orders — the real spread will be wider than the binomial predicts. Never trust a formula you can't verify: simulating 100,000 days with rng.binomial gives 0.2679 for exactly 3 returns, close to the exact 0.2668 — the small gap is just simulation noise.

When you count events in a fixed window arriving independently at a steady average rate, use Poisson, with a single parameter lambda. Say a help desk averages 4 tickets per hour: a silent hour happens under 2 percent of the time, exactly 4 tickets about 19.5 percent, and 8 or more tickets about 5.1 percent of the time.

A distinctive Poisson feature: mean and variance are both equal to lambda. If your real count data has a variance far above its mean — called overdispersion — Poisson is the wrong model. Poisson is also the limit of a binomial with huge n and tiny p: a binomial of 1000 trials at p equals 0.004 gives almost exactly the same answer as Poisson with lambda 4.

If each visitor converts with probability 0.2, how many visitors until the first conversion? That's geometric. The first conversion lands on visitor 3 about 12.8 percent of the time, and on average you wait 1 over p, or 5 visitors, for the first success.

To pick the right one, ask three questions: is it one trial or many? Are you counting successes out of a known n — binomial — counting events in a window with no fixed n — Poisson — or waiting for the first success — geometric? Then check independence honestly.

To recap: Bernoulli is one trial, binomial counts successes, Poisson counts events in a window, and geometric counts trials to the first success — scipy gives pmf, cdf, and sf for all of them, and simulation confirms your reading. Next, we meet the single most important continuous distribution: the normal distribution.
